Here’s a cohesive, ready-to-deliver 12-week general strength program for your client, incorporating spinal-safety constraints (no heavy spinal loading or loaded spinal flexion), a dual cardio plan, a structured abs/core progression, a sleep & recovery protocol, the anti-inflammatory nutrition guidance, and the requested updates (phase structure, weekly layout, and testing in Week 12). The plan is written for a 4-days-per-week training frequency (A, B, C, D) with 2 cardio days and built-in deloads. I’ve included week-by-week structure, exercise selections, sets, reps, RPE targets, and progression notes, plus safety cues.

Overall plan at a glance
- Phase 1: Foundation & technique (Weeks 1–4)
  - Emphasis: technique, core bracing, establishing work capacity, safe movement patterns
  - 4 training days (A lower, B upper, C lower, D upper) + 2 cardio days
- Phase 2: Strength build (Weeks 5–8)
  - Emphasis: increased loading on main lifts with preserved spinal safety
  - Push intensity increased (as requested) within safe RPE ranges
  - 4 training days + 2 cardio days
- Phase 3: Intensity & consolidation (Weeks 9–12)
  - Emphasis: peak strength development, controlled progression, and a 1RM testing window in Week 12
  - 4 training days + 2 cardio days
- Abs/core integrated throughout, with a progressive anti-extension/anti-rotation focus
- Sleep & recovery, anti-inflammatory nutrition, and cardio designed to support strength gains and disc health

Phase 1: Foundation & technique (Weeks 1–4)

Week 1
- Day A – Lower
  - Back Squat or Goblet Squat: 3 x 5 at moderate load (RPE 7)
  - Romanian Deadlift (RDL) from floor or long-arc: 3 x 6
  - Hip hinge mobility: 2 x 10 per side
  - Glute bridge or hip thrust: 3 x 8
  - Farmer’s carry: 3 x 30s
- Day B – Upper
  - Barbell bench press or floor press: 3 x 6
  - Barbell row: 3 x 6
  - Dumbbell shoulder press: 3 x 8
  - Lat pulldown: 3 x 8
  - Pallof press: 3 x 8 per side
- Day C – Lower
  - Leg press or beltless squat: 3 x 8
  - Hip hinge accessory: 3 x 8
  - Split squat or reverse lunge: 3 x 8 per leg
  - Core: side plank 3 x 30–45s per side
- Day D – Upper
  - Incline dumbbell press or incline barbell: 3 x 8
  - Seated cable row: 3 x 8
  - Face pulls: 3 x 12
  - Dumbbell lateral raises: 3 x 12
  - Pallof press: 3 x 10 per side
- Cardio: 2 sessions/wk, 20–25 min each (Zone 2)
  - Week 1: Walks with incline segments + light cycle

Week 2
- Similar structure; increase load ~2–5% on main lifts if technique solid; aim for RPE 7–8 on primary sets
- Cardio as Week 1, with minor progression (e.g., 1 more minute or slightly longer incline segments)

Week 3
- Deload concept: reduce volume ~20–30% or replace one hard set with tempo work (3–0–3–0)
- Technique-focused; keep loads conservative
- Cardio: maintain 20–25 min, keep Zone 2

Week 4
- Rebuild to Week 1 loads or small progression; ensure core bracing and neutral spine
- Cardio: Week 4 similar to Week 2 if tolerance supports

Phase 2: Strength build (Weeks 5–8)

Week 5
- Day A – Lower
  - Back Squat: 4 x 5 (RPE 7–8)
  - Romanian Deadlift: 3 x 5
  - Hip thrust/Glute bridge: 3 x 8
  - Farmer’s carry: 3 x 40–50m
  - Core: dead bug 3 x 8 per side
- Day B – Upper
  - Bench Press: 4 x 5 (increase load ~2.5–5% from Week 4 if solid)
  - Barbell Row: 3 x 6
  - Lat pulldown / Weighted chin-up: 3 x 6–8
  - Overhead Dumbbell Press: 3 x 8
  - Face pulls: 3 x 12
- Day C – Lower
  - Front Squat or beltless squat: 3–4 x 5
  - Hip hinge accessory: 3 x 6
  - Bulgarian Split Squat: 3 x 6 per leg
  - Core: anti-rotation drill 3 x 8 per side
- Day D – Upper
  - Overhead Press: 4 x 5
  - Pendlay Row or chest-supported row: 3 x 6
  - Incline Dumbbell Press: 3 x 8
  - Band Pull-Apart: 3 x 12
  - Triceps Pushdown: 3 x 10

Week 6
- Progression: add 2.5–5% to main pushes if technique remains solid; aim for RPE 7–8
- Keep spine safe cues; if fatigue accumulates, scale back one accessory

Week 7
- Density focus; maintain loads but increase work capacity
  - Example: A: Squats 4 x 5 at 7–8; add 1 back-off set if form allows
  - B: Bench 4 x 5 at 7–8; optional post-fatigue set at 6
  - C: Front Squat 3–4 x 5; slightly heavier accessories
  - D: Overhead Press 4 x 5; tempo 2–0–2–0 for 2–3 sets if stable

Week 8
- Deload week: reduce overall training stress by 30–40%; maintain technique and mobility work
- Optional light cardio and mobility emphasis

Phase 3: Intensity & consolidation (Weeks 9–12)

Week 9
- Day A – Lower
  - Back Squat: 4 x 4 at RPE 8
  - Romanian Deadlift: 3 x 4
  - Hip thrust: 3 x 6
  - Farmer’s carry: 3 x 50–60m
  - Core: dead bug variations
- Day B – Upper
  - Bench Press: 4 x 4
  - Barbell Row: 4 x 5
  - Weighted Pull-up or Lat Pulldown: 3 x 6
  - Overhead Press: 3 x 6
  - Face pulls: 3 x 12
- Day C – Lower
  - Front Squat or Safety-bar squat: 4 x 4
  - Hip hinge: 3 x 5
  - Bulgarian Split Squat: 3 x 6 per leg
  - Core: weighted carries 3 x 30s
- Day D – Upper
  - Incline Bench or DB Press: 4 x 4
  - Seated Row / Chest-supported Row: 4 x 6
  - Lateral Raises: 3 x 12
  - Band Pull-Aparts: 3 x 15
  - Triceps extension: 3 x 10

Week 10
- Progressive overload if technique allows; otherwise maintain Week 9 loads
- Maintain RPE 7–8 on main lifts

Week 11
- Peak-strength approach:
  - Back Squat: 3–4 x 3 at high quality
  - Bench: 3–4 x 3–4
  - Rows: 3–4 x 4–6
  - Optional light upper back work and anti-rotation drills

Week 12 — 1RM testing window
- Focus: safe, structured 1RM testing with warm-up and contingency plans
- Lifts to test: Primary picks based on Week 9–11 performance and comfort
  - Back Squat or Front Squat
  - Bench Press or Floor Press
  - Overhead Press
  - Optional: Deadlift alternative (Trap-Bar) only if clinically appropriate
- Testing order (recommended): Bench/Overhead Press first; then Squat; optional Deadlift
- Warm-up protocol: 5–10 min general warm-up, then gradually increase load with double/quad reps to prime CNS and refine technique
- Attempt progression: 3–5 attempts per lift; stop if technique degrades or pain appears; back off to last successful weight if necessary
- Post-testing: mobility and recovery emphasis; light cardio optional; resume standard training at Week 13 (or a recovery week if needed)

- Weeks 1–4: Pallof press, Dead Bug, Bird-Dog, Side Plank, Anti-rotation carries
- Weeks 5–8: Add Hanging knee raises or leg raises subbed with regression if needed; progress to Ab wheel rollout only if bracing is solid
- Weeks 9–12: Maintain core without compromising spinal safety; include anti-rotation carries and planks with variations (tempo holds, marching feet)

Cardio (2 sessions per week)
- Phase 1: 20–25 min at Zone 2
- Phase 2: 25–30 min at Zone 2, with optional light Zone 3 bursts occasionally
- Phase 3: 25–35 min at Zone 2; one short higher-output interval (e.g., 6 x 20s hard / 40s easy) if recovered
- Modal options: incline walking, cycling, elliptical, rower
- Scheduling: keep cardio after lower-body sessions or on separate days; lighter after upper-body sessions or on rest days

Sleep & recovery protocol
- Sleep target: 7–9 hours per night, aim for 7.5–8.5 hours most nights
- Consistent schedule, sleep environment optimization, pre-sleep routine (breathing, mobility)
- Hydration and nutrition timing to support sleep quality
- Weekly deloads in Weeks 4, 8, 12 with added mobility/relaxation

Anti-inflammatory nutrition
- Protein: 1.6–2.0 g/kg/day
- Calories: maintain or modestly adjust to training
- Daily structure: protein at each meal; anti-inflammatory foods: fatty fish, olive oil, leafy greens, berries, cruciferous vegetables; spices (turmeric, ginger), garlic
- Probiotics: yogurt/kefir/ferments or supplement if needed
- Hydration: 30–40 ml/kg/day plus around training
- Weekly meal templates provided in general plan; 2–3 anti-inflammatory meals per day baseline; rotate meals to maintain adherence

1RM testing readiness & safety notes
- Prioritize clinician guidance; ensure no new symptoms
- Use a ramp warm-up and conservative attempts
- Have a spotter and safety equipment; belt use per clinician guidance
- If pain occurs, revert to prior submax loads and re-test later

Progression and safety cues
- Primary progression: small load increases on main lifts when technique is solid and symptoms absent
- If symptoms occur, reduce volume/loads and consult clinician
- Maintain neutral spine on all lifts; anti-extension and anti-rotation core program emphasized

Deliverables you can hand to the client

- 1RM testing sheet and safety protocol for Week 12

- Quick-start sleep & recovery guide and a simple weekly recovery checklist

For someone with a prior L4-L5 disc herniation, the goal is to train the core for stability and bracing without loading the spine in flexion, shear, or rotation that could irritate the disc. We’ll prioritize anti-extension and anti-rotation core work, plus progressive bracing and controlled breathing. Here’s a safe, progressive abs plan you can integrate into the existing 12-week program.

Core training principles for this client
- Favor anti-extension (spine-stable) and anti-rotation drills rather than full loaded spinal flexion.
- Use bracing cues: “brace, breathe, maintain neutral spine.” Exhale with effort to help bracing.
- Start with low loading and high control; progress only when technique is solid and there are no symptoms.
- Integrate core work on lower-load days or after main lifts when the spine is already braced from lifting.

Weeks 1–4 (Foundation)
- Pallof press (standing or kneeling) – 3 x 8–10 per side
  - Cues: tall posture, brace core, push resistance away from the center, avoid twisting torso.
- Dead bug – 3 x 8–10 per side
  - Cues: keep lower back pressed to floor, slow controlled limb movements, maintain neutral spine.
- Bird-dog – 3 x 8 per side
  - Cues: hold range briefly, avoid sagging hips; slow tempo.
- Side plank (progression) – 3 x 20–30 seconds per side
  - If it aggravates hips, reduce to 15–20 seconds or replace with side-forearm planks on the floor with knee down.
- Farmer’s carry or suitcase carry (as part of existing carries) – 2–3 x 30–45 seconds
  - Rationale: anti-rotational loading with bracing, works the whole core in a functional way.

Weeks 5–8 (Strengthening)
- Pallof press – 3 x 10–12 per side (increase resistance or stance widen)
- Dead bug – 3 x 12 per side
- Hanging leg raise regression: knee taps to chest or tuck holds on a bar (if tolerated) – 3 x 6–8
  - If straight leg raises cause spine flexion or pain, do a supine lying leg raise with a slight knee bend or a cable-assisted version, but stop if pain.
- Ab wheel rollouts (if trunk bracing is solid and no symptoms) – 2 x 6–8
  - Alternative: slabbed rollout with ab wheel on knees or use a barbell roll-out with cautious depth
- Plank progression: front plank 3 x 30–40 seconds; add tempo (4–0–2–0) if stable
- Side planks with hip in line – 3 x 25–35 seconds per side
  - Progression: can add a tiny reach (opposite hand to ankle) only if form remains solid.

Weeks 9–12 (Maintenance and selection)
- Pallof press – 3 x 12–15 per side, increased resistance
- Dead bug – 3 x 12–15 per side with a slower tempo
- Hanging knee raises or elevated knee raises – 3 x 8–10
- Ab wheel rollout or barbell rollout – 2 x 8–10 (only if no pain and technique flawless)
- Front plank variations: treadmill incline back extension holds, dragon flag progressions only if confident (these are advanced; otherwise maintain planks)
- Side planks with marching feet – 3 x 20–30 seconds per side
- Optional anti-rotation band walks ( Pallof-light) or cable anti-rotation presses as cue-based finisher 2 x 10 per side

Modifications and substitutions
- If any movement triggers back pain, drop it and substitute with a safer alternative:
  - Replace leg raises with bent-k knee variations or supported knee-ins on a bench.
  - Replace ab wheel with stability ball rollouts limited range.
- If symptoms flare, revert to Weeks 1–4 baseline and reduce tempo, sets, and intensity.

Integration with the plan
- Frequency: 2–3 core sessions per week integrated into your existing A/B/C/D schedule as short 5–12 minute blocks after lifting or on dedicated core days.
- Order: place core work after the main lifts when possible to avoid compromising lifting performance, or on a separate short day if needed.
- Progression rule: increase reps or resistance only when you can perform all reps with neutral spine and controlled tempo without pain.

Cues and coaching tips
- breath cadence: inhale to brace, exhale through exertion, maintaining neutral spine throughout.
- brace cue: “ribcage down, belly button to spine, glutes engaged.”
- cue for anti-rotation: keep hips square, avoid torso twisting when pressing or pulling.

Sample 1-week micro-structure
- Day after lower body lift: Pallof press 3 x 10 per side, Dead bug 3 x 12, Side plank 3 x 25s per side
- Day after upper body lift: Plank 3 x 30–40s, Bird-dog 3 x 8 per side, Pallof press 3 x 12 per side
- Optional cardio days: add light core activation with stability work if energy allows (no direct spine loading)

Safety reminders
- If any new back pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness occurs, stop the exercise and reassess with your client. If symptoms persist, consult the client’s clinician.
- Never perform core work with heavy spinal flexion under load or with poor bracing.
- Ensure warm-up includes hip mobility and thoracic spine mobility to support bracing and posture.

Understood. Adding a safe, structured 1RM testing protocol for the final week (Week 12) can give you a clear performance benchmark while respecting his disc history and the phase progression. The plan below preserves safety, aligns with Phase 3 (“Intensity & consolidation”), and minimizes risk by using a controlled ramping approach and built-in warm-up, technique checks, and contingency steps.

Key testing principles
- Prioritize safety: ensure neutral spine, bracing, no reported symptoms, and proper warm-up before attempting any heavy lift.
- Test after a light/energy-treshing day or at least 2–3 days after the heaviest lifting days to minimize fatigue impact.
- Use conservative 1RM estimation methods if needed (e.g., perform a single-rep max test on a lift with an established pattern and a recent progression), with a plan to back off if form or pain arises.
- Maintain a conservative plan for the surrounding days; avoid high-volume or high-intensity sessions the same day as a 1RM test.

Where 1RM testing fits in Phase 3
- Weeks 9–11: peak strength development and taper toward Week 12.
- Week 12: testing window, with a precise schedule for lifts to be tested (prioritize main strength lifts with stable technique already in the program).

Proposed Week 12 structure (with testing day)
- Mon: Lower focus (light to moderate work for warm-up, not fatigue-heavy). Technical prep only.
- Tue: Upper focus (technical work and warm-up; no heavy loading beyond planned loads for that week).
- Thu: 1RM testing session (primary lifts identified; see below).
- Fri/Sat: Mobility/Recovery and optional light cardio; rest days as needed.

1RM testing plan: which lifts to test and progression
- Primary candidates:
  - Back Squat or Front Squat (choose the one used most consistently throughout the program)
  - Bench Press or Floor Press (depending on preference and comfort)
  - Overhead Press (strict press or push-press if shoulder tolerance is good; otherwise strict OHP)
- Secondary lift optional: Deadlift is typically riskier with disc history; consider a safe lower-back-friendly pull test only if you’ve ensured prior weeks’ progression and no symptoms. If tested, use a conservative protocol (e.g., trap-bar deadlift alternative in Week 12).
- Testing order to reduce fatigue: Start with the best technique and lowest fatigue-lurking lift, usually Bench or Overhead Press, then Squat, then the remaining.

Testing protocol (example)
- General approach: ramp warm-up to a top single, then attempt a true 1RM with safety and form checks.
- Warm-up sequence (adjust weights to client’s numbers):
  - Barbell work weight (e.g., empty bar, 20–40% of a rough estimated 1RM) x 5–8 reps
  - Add weights in small increments (e.g., 10–20 lb / 5–10 kg) with 2–4 reps per set, 2–4 minutes rest between sets
  - Final singles at modest increments until a true 1RM attempt is reached
- Attempt cadence:
  - If the rep quality remains high (technique solid, bracing intact, no pain), attempt the next load.
  - If form breaks or pain occurs, back off to the previous successful attempt and consider that as the 1RM for that lift (or stop testing that lift entirely if symptoms arise).
- Number of attempts:
  - 3–5 attempts per lift maximum. If you’re not progressing safely, stop earlier and assign a “best successful single” from the last good attempt.

Safety considerations and adjustments for disc history
- Do not test a lift if there is any new or lingering back pain, radicular symptoms, or instability.
- Use a power rack with safety pins/bars in place. Have a spotter or training partner present, especially for bench and squats.
- For the bench press, use a lifting belt only if recommended by the clinician; otherwise keep core bracing stable without belt to avoid unnecessary spinal load.
- For overhead press, ensure a stable base and no excessive spinal extension; consider using dumbbell OHP to reduce axial loading if barbell OHP feels less stable.
- If the client is not ready for a true 1RM due to risk, skip the 1RM and perform a 3–5RM test or estimated 1RM via rep-max testing (e.g., 5RM) and use a validated formula (Epley, Brzycki, etc.) to estimate 1RM.

Integration with Week 9–11 plan
- Weeks 9–11: taper and peak approach for main lifts; maintain form and technique while gradually pushing heavier loads in a controlled fashion.
- Week 11: final load check and readiness assessment; if the client demonstrates solid technique and no pain, proceed with Week 12 testing.
- Week 12: perform the 1RM tests in a pre-planned order; ensure the day includes adequate warm-up and cooldown, plus post-test mobility and recovery.

Example test schedule (one possible plan)
- Monday Week 12: Lower lift testing window
  - Warm-up: mobility + light sets
  - Back Squat 1RM attempt #1
  - If successful and form solid, attempt 1RM #2
  - If failure occurs, record last successful attempt as actual 1RM and stop for that lift
- Tuesday Week 12: Upper lift testing window
  - Bench Press 1RM attempt(s) following same ramp protocol
- Thursday Week 12: Overhead Press testing
  - OHP 1RM attempt(s)
- Optional: Friday Week 12 or the following day: Deadlift test only if appropriate after a thorough review with the client and clinician

Notes for the client handout
- Before testing, rest well and fuel appropriately; avoid heavy cardio the day before.
- Ensure a proper warm-up and clear communication with the trainer if any pain or discomfort arises.
- After testing, allow for 48–72 hours of recovery before resuming full training volume.

Deliverables for you as the trainer
- A Week 12 testing plan with exact lifts, warm-up scheme, target load progression strategy, and safety cues.
- A simple 1RM testing log sheet for sessions, including warm-up reps/loads, single attempt weights, and outcome (success/failure).
- Quick-reference safety cues and a flowchart for what to do if pain or symptoms arise during testing.

Here’s a practical, client-ready plan you can drop into the 12-week program. It covers sleep targets, pre-sleep routines, daily recovery practices, and weekly deload/active recovery blocks.

1) Sleep targets and environment
- Daily sleep goal: 7–9 hours, aiming for 7.5–8.5 on most nights.
- Consistent schedule: same bedtime and wake time within ±1 hour, including weekends.
- Sleep environment: cool (60–67°F / 15–19°C), dark (use blackout curtains or eye mask), quiet or with a white-noise source.
- Pre-sleep electronics: limit screen time 60 minutes before bed; if using devices, enable blue-light reduction and use dim lighting.
- Sleep surface: medium-firm mattress, supportive pillow that keeps neck neutral.

2) Pre-sleep routine (20–40 minutes)
- Light mobility: 5 minutes total body mobility focusing on hips, thoracic spine, and shoulders.
- Relaxation practice: 5–10 minutes of breathing work or meditation (box breathing 4s inhale, 4s hold, 4s exhale, 4s hold).
- Wind-down activity: reading a book, gentle stretching, or a warm bath/shower (temperature drop afterward aids sleep onset).
- Caffeine timing: avoid caffeine after 2:00 pm or 6 hours before bedtime.
- Alcohol: minimize intake; if consumed, do so earlier in the evening and keep amount modest as it disrupts sleep quality.

3) Daily recovery habits (12-month view, with training days weighted)
- Hydration: maintain hydration throughout the day; color of urine should be pale straw.
- Nutrition timing: protein at regular intervals; avoid large meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime; a small, easily digestible snack (e.g., casein-rich or a small yogurt) can help sleep if needed.
- Post-training recovery window: immediate 20–40 g protein and 20–40 g carbohydrate within 1–2 hours post-workout; continue hydration to offset sweat losses.
- Daily movement: 8–10k steps or step-equivalent activity on non-training days; light mobility or gentle walking can aid sleep quality.
- Light exposure: get natural light in the morning (10–20 minutes) to support circadian rhythm; outdoors preferred if possible.

4) Recovery modalities integrated into the plan
- Soft-tissue work: 1 session per week focusing on hips, thoracic spine, and calves (30–45 minutes total), using foam rolling and self-myofascial release.
- Mobility work: short daily routines (5–8 minutes) targeting thoracic mobility, hip flexor length, ankle dorsiflexion, and scapular hygiene.
- Cryotherapy or contrast baths: optional, 1–2 times per week for 5–10 minutes after training if available and comfortable; otherwise skip.
- Warm-ups: include dynamic mobility and activation drills before every session to reduce the risk of aggravation.

5) Weekly recovery structure
- Deload weeks (Weeks 4, 8, 12): intensify the recovery focus during these weeks, with:
  - Slightly reduced daily training stress (volume cut by 20–30% or intensity reduced by 1–2 RPE levels).
  - Additional dedicated sleep/relaxation practices on non-lifting days.
  - Increased emphasis on mobility work and light cardio as active recovery.
- Active recovery days: two light cardio sessions or mobility days per week, not exhausting, to promote blood flow and recovery without interfering with strength work.

6) Monitoring and progression
- Sleep tracking: encourage simple logs (bedtime, wake time, perceived sleep quality 1–5) or use a wearables-derived sleep score if the client uses a device.
- Recovery checklist (weekly): rate fatigue, muscle soreness, mood, and energy on a 1–5 scale; if sustained fatigue >3 days, reassess training load and sleep plan.
- Red flags: persistent insomnia (>2 weeks), waking unrefreshed, or daytime sleepiness interfering with daily life; if present, coordinate with healthcare professional to assess for sleep disorders or other medical issues.

7) Integration with the existing plan
- Place sleep and recovery guidance as a parallel track to strength programming.
- Use “recovery days” in the schedule to ensure rest is built-in; avoid stacking high-demand sessions back-to-back if the client is still adapting.
- For the 1RM testing week, plan extra recovery: two light cardio days or rest days surrounding the testing window; prioritize sleep the nights before the test.

8) Quick-start starter tips (handy to give client)
- Aim for a consistent wake time even on weekends.
- Create a 20–30 minute wind-down ritual that you actually do every night.
- Track sleep quality 3–4 weeks; if not meeting targets, adjust bedtime by 15–30 minutes earlier.
- If stress spikes, add 5–10 minutes of breathing work or light mobility before bed and consider an earlier bedtime.
